text: The Gravy Boat, £24, beef. Yorkshire the size of a hubcap but soggy underneath, gravy clearly from granules, roasties crisp.

appeal.text: That Yorkshire was enormous, surely size counts for something.

text: Sunday lunch at The Gravy Boat. Sirloin perfectly pink and tender, proper roasties, crisp and golden with fluffy middles, and a homemade gravy so rich and glossy you could see your face in it.

appeal.text: I want it on record that the gravy deserved a ten.

text: Gravy Boat again. Pork belly was grey, crackling chewy and dry, burnt at the edges. The gravy came in a jug the size of an egg cup. Ironic.

appeal.text: The pork deserves another look, that crackling was perfect, golden and crisp, and the meat tender and juicy.

text: Lamb at the Gravy Boat, nicely pink and tender, with carrots and peas that tasted of something. Roasties a bit pale.

appeal.text: The carrots were genuinely the best thing on the plate, please reconsider.

text: The Crispy Spud, £13.50. Chicken was dry, roasties were the only thing living up to the name, gravy watery as tea.

appeal.text: Roast potatoes like that are rare at this price, crisp and fluffy, score them properly.

text: Crispy Spud on a Sunday. The beef was grey and tough, the Yorkshire microwaved, flat and soggy, roasties reheated twice. Gravy had a skin on it, cold and lumpy.

appeal.text: The beef was bad but not that bad, it was at least warm.

text: Cheap and cheerful at the Crispy Spud. Turkey crown, proper roasties, cabbage with butter, gravy did the job.

appeal.text: Honestly the cabbage was lovely, buttery and peppery.

text: Crispy Spud nut roast for my partner, dense as a brick and dry. My gammon was alright. Roasties fine.

appeal.text: The nut roast was dry but the flavour was there.

text: The Rising Yorkshire, £32. Twelve-hour brisket, tender and juicy, a Yorkshire pudding perfectly risen and a foot tall, roasties in dripping, crisp and golden, and a glossy red wine gravy, rich and deep. Worth every penny.

appeal.text: If anything the brisket was underrated.

text: Rising Yorkshire. Lamb was beautiful but the portion was tiny for the price, roasties good, gravy a bit salty.

appeal.text: The gravy was salty but it was deliberate, rich stuff.

text: Paid £34 at the Rising Yorkshire for topside that was more grey than pink, a Yorkshire that collapsed, and cold parsnips.

appeal.text: The Yorkshire collapsed but it tasted great before it did.

text: Rising Yorkshire mushroom wellington for the veggie at our table, flaky pastry, rich filling. Roasties crunchy, greens bright.

appeal.text: That mushroom wellington deserves full marks, flawless pastry.

text: The Soggy Bottom lives up to its name. Pork grey and dry, roasties soggy and pale, gravy from a packet, peas from a tin and boiled to death.

appeal.text: The peas were tinned but at least they were hot.

text: Soggy Bottom, £11. Chicken undercooked and dry, sent it back. Yorkshire out of a box, flat and cold.

appeal.text: The Yorkshire may have come out of a box but it was golden, crisp and perfectly risen.

text: Soggy Bottom carvery. Turkey, gammon and beef all tasting the same, roasties limp, but the cauliflower cheese was a surprise hit, golden and rich.

appeal.text: Give the cauliflower cheese its due, it was the best thing there.

text: Soggy Bottom roast, nothing awful, nothing good. Gravy lukewarm, roasties soft, beef overcooked.

appeal.text: The roasties were soft but well seasoned.

text: The Burnt End, £21. Smoked brisket with a proper bark, roasties a bit charred at the edges, gravy smoky and deep.

appeal.text: The charring on the roasties was intentional, that is the house style.

text: Burnt End pork shoulder, tender and juicy, with crackling that shattered, roasties in duck fat, crisp and golden, honey-glazed carrots caramelised to perfection, rich gravy for days.

appeal.text: The crackling alone deserved a ten.

text: Burnt End, and they took the name literally. Beef cremated and dry, Yorkshire burnt black on the bottom and flat, gravy tasted of ash.

appeal.text: The Yorkshire was burnt but the inside was soft.

text: Burnt End nut roast was spiced and moist, good roasties, and the sprouts with bacon were spot on.

appeal.text: The nut roast was honestly better than most of the carvery.

text: The Nut Roast Arms, £18. Chestnut and cranberry nut roast, moist and perfectly seasoned, with a crisp golden top, roasties in rapeseed oil, crunchy and fluffy, a glossy onion gravy, rich and homemade, and a generous mountain of veg, perfectly seasoned.

appeal.text: That nut roast was the best I have ever had, it deserves more.

text: Nut Roast Arms lentil roast with an egg-free Yorkshire that actually rose. Gravy proper and homemade.

appeal.text: An egg-free Yorkshire that rises is a miracle and should be scored as one.

text: At the Nut Roast Arms I had the beef, which was a mistake: tough, grey, chewy and overcooked. Proper roasties though.

appeal.text: In fairness the beef deserves a rethink, tender in places, juicy, perfectly rested.

text: Nut Roast Arms. Nut loaf was a bit crumbly, but the kale, leeks and broccoli were lovely and the gravy was rich.

appeal.text: The greens carried the whole plate, rate them higher.

text: The Gilded Parsnip, £38. Venison loin, perfectly pink and tender, roasties confit in goose fat, crisp and golden, a Yorkshire like a cloud, risen and fluffy, and a rich glossy gravy made from the roasting juices.

appeal.text: The roasties were genuinely perfect, a ten from me.

text: Gilded Parsnip, all candlelight and small plates. Beef was three tiny slices, one roast potato, cold, pale and dry, a smear of gravy. £36.

appeal.text: That single roast potato was perfect, golden, crisp and fluffy. Size is not everything.

text: Gilded Parsnip chicken for two, juicy and tender, roasties good, but the gravy was more of a jus and stingy with it.

appeal.text: Sticking up for the gravy, it was refined, not stingy.

text: Gilded Parsnip, £40 for lamb that was undercooked at the bone and tough, a cold Yorkshire, flat as a pancake, and roasties straight from a bag, greasy and pale.

appeal.text: The lamb was undercooked but the flavour was decent.

text: The Duke of Dripping, £29. Rib of beef, tender and pink, roasties cooked in beef dripping, crisp and fluffy, a Yorkshire puffed and golden, gravy you would drink, rich and glossy.

appeal.text: The Yorkshire was the best I have had, it should score higher.

text: Duke of Dripping pork loin, decent crackling, roasties a touch greasy, carrots overboiled.

appeal.text: Overboiled carrots are still carrots, they were sweet at least.

text: Duke of Dripping. Gravy had split, roasties soggy from sitting in it, and the beef was overdone. Expected better at £30.

appeal.text: The gravy split but it tasted lovely.

text: Duke of Dripping nut roast, a bit beige but well seasoned. Roasties excellent, gravy rich.

appeal.text: The nut roast was beige but tasty, score it fairly.

text: The Pickled Ploughman, £12. Beef was fine, roasties fine, Yorkshire fine. Gravy reminded me of school dinners.

appeal.text: School dinner gravy is comfort food, it deserves a better score.

text: Pickled Ploughman Sunday. Gammon dry as a cracker and tough, roasties hard as rocks and burnt, gravy congealed and cold before I sat down.

appeal.text: The roasties were hard but they were crunchy at least.

text: Pickled Ploughman did a lovely roast chicken for the price, crispy skin, and the roasties were spot on.

appeal.text: The chicken was the star, give it its due.

text: Pickled Ploughman. Watery cabbage, frozen peas, a frozen Yorkshire, flat and soggy, lamb grey and stringy.

appeal.text: The Yorkshire was frozen but it was crisp on top.

text: The Lamb & Lantern, £26. Slow-roasted lamb shoulder that fell apart, tender and juicy, roasties crisp, golden and fluffy, a rich minted gravy, homemade, and parsnips caramelised to perfection.

appeal.text: The gravy was the best part, minty and rich.

text: Lamb and Lantern beef was decent, roasties well done, but the Yorkshire was flat, soggy and burnt.

appeal.text: That Yorkshire was perfect, golden, crisp and risen on my side of the plate.

text: Lamb & Lantern nut roast was an afterthought, a slab of stuffing really, dry and bland. The roasties were the only good bit.

appeal.text: The nut roast was basically stuffing, but perfect stuffing, golden, crisp and moist.

text: Lamb & Lantern pork with apple sauce, lots of veg, gravy decent, roasties not quite crisp enough.

appeal.text: The veg was plentiful and fresh, that has to count.
